title: Report of a Leprosy case in Singapore: an age-old disease not to be forgotten in developed countries with low-prevalence settings
case_text:
A Filipino male in his 30s presented with a persistent non-tender erythematous plaque over his right upper back for many years. It began as a faint erythema that slowly developed into a ring-like plaque lesion. It was non-pruritic in nature and the plaque did not respond to topical antifungal treatment. He had this skin lesion prior to arriving in Singapore but decided to seek medical attention as the lesion progressed with new erythematous papules developing over the face, trunk and upper limbs in the past 2 months. There was no prior trauma or irritants applied to the skin and the patient did not complain of any systemic symptoms of fever, loss of weight and night sweat. There was no numbness or weakness and he did not have another co-existing medical condition. He denied ingestion of medication and sexual contact with a commercial sexual worker. The patient came to Singapore 7 years ago to work as nursing personnel and travelled back to the Philippines once to twice a year to visit his family. His housemate and family members did not have any skin complaint.
On physical examination, there was a large well demarcated annular plaque of 10 by 7.5 cm over the right upper back, which extended to the axilla (Fig. 1a). It was erythematous, infiltrated and not scaly. There were also multiple monomorphic papules of 0.5 to 1 cm in size over the upper limbs (Fig. 1b), face, proximal aspect of lower limbs and the gluteal region. Punch biopsies of the skin lesions were taken from the plaque at the back and one of the papules at the upper limb. Microscopic examination of the skin biopsies revealed a diffuse superficial dermal infiltrate of epithelioid histiocytes without well-formed granulomas surrounded by lymphocytes or any multinucleate Langhans giant cells. Foamy cytoplasm was seen in only a portion of the histiocytes and was subtle (Fig. 2a, b). Fite-positive bacilli were identified within the inflammatory infiltrate (Fig. 2c). All the controls demonstrated appropriate reactivity. In view of the histopathological findings, the microbiologists were consulted and deparaffinized samples from the skin lesions were sent for non-tuberculous mycobacteria (NTM) and leprosy molecular testing, which were performed using commercially available line-probe assays INNO-LiPA Mycobacteria v2 (Innogenetics, Belgium) and GenoType LepraeDR v1 (Hain LifeScience, Germany), respectively. The result was positive for  M. leprae  with no mutation detected at rpoB (rifampicin), gyrA (ofloxacin) and folP1 (dapsone) gene targets by the assay.

distillation_prompt.system_prompt:
You are an expert clinician–educator in tropical and infectious diseases.
Your job is to transform a published clinical case report into a standardized admission diagnostic teaching case following the Stanford MedCaseReasoning methodology.

In terms of style, model your output on NEJM’s Clinicopathologic Conferences ("Case Records of the Massachusetts General Hospital").

RULES (Read Carefully — No Exceptions):
1. SOURCE FIDELITY:
   - Extract facts ONLY from the supplied case report.
   - Do NOT invent, embellish, or smooth out missing clinical data.
   - Never extrapolate findings not explicitly mentioned.

2. THE ADMISSION BREAKPOINT PRINCIPLE (CRITICAL):
   - The <case_prompt> represents what an emergency triage clinician knows on Day 1 BEFORE confirmatory tests return.
   - INCLUDE in <case_prompt>: Demographics, travel/occupational/vector exposures (freshwater contact, insect bites, animal exposure), symptom chronology, vital signs, physical exam findings, and initial triage laboratory/imaging results (CBC, platelets, basic metabolic panel, LFTs, urinalysis, plain chest radiograph, bedside ultrasound).
   - STRICTLY EXCLUDE from <case_prompt>:
     * Any mention of the disease name or pathogen genus/species (e.g., do not write "Leptospirosis", "Burkholderia", "Leishmania", "Paragonimus").
     * Confirmatory send-out PCR panels, serological titers, blood culture organism identifications, or biopsy histopathology.
     * The clinical outcome or treatment response (these belong in the diagnostic reasoning, not the presentation).

3. STRUCTURE OF <diagnostic_reasoning>:
   - Enumerate all alternative candidate diagnoses considered in the text.
   - For each candidate, provide a concise summary explaining why it was considered and why it was ruled out in this patient, followed by a direct verbatim quote from the article in quotation marks.
   - Conclude with the Diagnostic Pivot: the pivotal clinical and confirmatory turning point that established the confirmed diagnosis.

4. TARGET CANONICAL DISEASE:
   - The verified ground-truth disease for this patient is: Leprosy
   - Disease subtype / specific manifestation: leprosy
